senses: A container from which fluids are intended to be drunk, having one handle and usually a base in the form of a head.
A Thracian drinking horn.
ety: Ancient Greek ῥυτόν (rhutón), ultimately from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”)

senses: Bullous; involving large blisters.
ety: From Latin bullosa via the influence of New Latin on medical terminology in modern languages.
examples: Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of mainly inherited connective tissue diseases that cause blisters in the skin and mucous membranes.

senses: The scientific study of spores, pollen and particulate organic matter in various matrices including the air (pollen counts), crime scenes, and sedimentary rocks.
A thick resistant particle produced by a bacterium or protist to survive in harsh or unfavorable conditions.
ety: From New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”), related to σπόρος (spóros, “sowing”) and σπείρω (speírō, “to sow”). Related to English spread).

senses: Having more than one syllable.
examples: But it’s a dialect Fetter doesn’t know. It sounds old, rolling and multisyllabic and liquid.

senses: Consisting of a peculiar form of words.
Synonym of manipulable (“suitable for, or able to be subjected to, manipulation”).
ety: From manipulate + -able (suffix meaning ‘able or fit to be done’ forming adjectives).

senses: To lay an impost upon.
To cause to pay tallage.
ety: From French taillage, from tailler (“to cut”).

senses: having a rough, surly, and harsh demeanor and nature.
hoarse-voiced.
ety: 16th century, from Dutch grof and/or Middle Low German grof (both “rough, coarse, rude”), from Old Dutch *grof or Old Saxon *grof, both from Proto-West Germanic *grob, from Proto-Germanic *grubaz (“coarse, rough”), possibly from an earlier *gahrubaz and then related with *hreubaz (“scabby, rough, scrubby”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian groaf (“rough, coarse, crude”), West Frisian grof (“rough, coarse, crude”), Low German groff (“rough, coarse, crude”), German grob (“rough, coarse, crude”), Swedish grov (“rough, coarse, crude”).

senses: Exhibiting piezoresistance.
To sterilize laboratory equipment in an autoclave.
ety: Borrowed from French autoclave, formed with prefix auto- + Latin clavis (“key”).

senses: Unable to be expressed; not able to be put into words.
examples: She felt inexpressible contempt for her attackers.
That noise, that awful clamour of uncouthness inexpressible, is the love-call of the storm bird!

She mixed furniture with the same fatal profligacy as she mixed drinks, and this outrageous contact between things which were intended by Nature to be kept poles apart gave her an inexpressible thrill.

senses: A modern ball game descended from tlachtli.
ety: Ultimately from Classical Nahuatl ōllamaliztli. Doublet of ullamaliztli.

senses: A division of land in India, usually a (small) subdivision of a pargana.
Someone who works in a livery stable.
Someone who wears livery in the course of their employment.
A member of a livery company.
A screw pine, screw palms (Pandanus spp.).
Traditional food flavouring derived from the leaves of Pandanus amaryllifolius.
ety: Borrowed from Malay pandan, ultimately from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *paŋdan. Doublet of hala via Hawaiian.

senses: Of a person or animal: pregnant
examples: Gestational mice were taken from the cage and divided into six groups by the draw lots method.

senses: One who makes, composes, or recites rhymes or simple poems.
ety: From Middle English rymare, from Old English rīmere (“a compouter, reckoner, calculator”), equivalent to rhyme + -er. Cognate with Dutch rijmer, German Reimer, Danish rimer, Swedish rimmare, Icelandic rímari. More at rhyme.

senses: One who barges or shoves.
The manager or driver of a barge.
An edible freshwater fish of the family Osphronemidae.
ety: From French gourami, from Malay gurami, from Javanese ꦒꦸꦫꦩꦶ (gurami).

senses: German-style shandy (drink of beer mixed with lemonade).
A traditional red or orange cosmetic powder from India, usually worn by Hindu women along the parting of the hair as a sign of marriage.
examples: After she’d brushed her hair and twisted it into a knot, she got her sindoor out of the cabinet. It was in a tiny, flat copper container, and the powder was bright red.

senses: The nightingale.
A musical instrument similar to the violin, but having four steel-wire strings.
examples: And lonely Philomel, still waking, sings.

senses: A member of a race of mythical fanged demons that eat human flesh and blood, somewhat like vampires.
examples: A race of one-eyed beings / All feared and shunned / Rakshasa demon

senses: One who couches paper.
The book in which a corporation or other body registers its particular acts.
ety: From Middle English coucher, from Anglo-Norman; equivalent to couch + -er.

senses: Photographic.
A residential school in India with pupils living near the guru, often in the same house.
The first compartment of the stomach of a cow or other ruminants.
Advisory; information; advice; intelligence.
A kind of dispatch boat or "advice boat", carrying orders before the development of effective remote communication; an advice boat, or dispatch boat.
A mid-sized colonial warship.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish aviso (“advice”). Doublet of advice.

senses: The mulberry fruit.
A tincture, the colour of mulberries, between gules (red) and purpure (purple).
ety: From Middle English murrey, murreye, from Middle French moré, morée, from Latin moratum, morata, from neuter and feminine respectively of moratus (“mulberry-colored”), from morum (“mulberry”) + -atus (“-ate”).

senses: A man who makes cheese.
Any of several nematode worms, of the family Oxyuridae, that are parasitic to mammals
The herb absinthium Artemisia absinthium (grande wormwood); essence of wormwood.
Bitterness; sorrow.
A distilled, highly alcoholic, anise-flavored liquor originally made from grande wormwood, anise, and other herbs.
A moderate yellow green.
absinthe green
ety: * (wormwood; figuratively bitterness, sorrow): From Middle English absinthe. * (liquor): From Modern French absinthe. Both from Middle French absinthe, from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion, “wormwood”). Doublet of absinthium.

senses: One who, or that which, stuffs.
A taxidermist.
Something which is stuffed into an enclosure, especially an advertising circular included with other mail.
One who conceals a package of illegal drugs by swallowing them.
Having crinkles; wrinkly.
Chinese steamed bun (without any filling)
ety: Borrowed from Mandarin 饅頭／馒头 (mántou). Doublet of mandu, manju, and manti.
examples: On nous apporta du thé, du riz et des mantous – des petits pains de farine de blé.

senses: That tends to assimilate
That tends to produce assimilation
examples: Some of the attested vocalic "monotony" can be explained by means of assimilatory processes within Sardinian.

senses: A public house that serves high-quality food.
examples: Indeed, one depressing thing about gastropubs is the lack of imagination in the sector; the way, as concepts, they invariably conform to a formulaic kind of low-key, small-g urban gentrification.
For many years, UK food had a terrible reputation. Then, in the 1990s, gastropubs brought new flavours, energy and ideas. When and why did it all start to go downhill again?

senses: Having (or having the characteristics associated with) a specified form of liver.
A conjectural statement or utterance.
ety: From Ancient Greek δοξασία (doxasía, “belief, opinion, conviction”).
